content.title: About
content.content: Egg, whole, fried with margarine is a classic dish made from a whole chicken egg cooked in vegetable fat. Frying creates a golden crust while margarine adds a mild buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is common in canteens and cafés across the former Soviet Union.
Margarine is used instead of butter because it is cheaper and has a longer shelf life.
A fried egg cooks quickly – usually 2–3 minutes in a pan.
In the 1930s, frying eggs in margarine was a popular, affordable home‑cooking method in Soviet households.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: The yolk is one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Contains choline
items.content: Choline supports liver function, brain health, and fat metabolism.

items.title: Contains lutein and zeaxanthin
items.content: These carotenoids promote eye health and may reduce the risk of age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Provides energy
items.content: Fats from margarine and protein from the egg deliver readily available energy.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: The yolk contains cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should consume in moderation.

items.title: Trans fats in margarine
items.content: Certain margarines may contain trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Over‑fried eggs can form acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried eggs can be served on their own, added to sandwiches, salads, rice or potato dishes, and are often garnished with fresh herbs or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best eaten immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 1–2 days in an airtight container and reheat before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy vegetable widely used in cooking. When prepared as NS as to form, cooked, it retains most nutrients while becoming tender and mildly flavored.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and has been cultivated for over 2,000 years.
The green color comes from chlorophyll, abundant in its leaves.
Several varieties exist: flat‑leaf, curly, and savoy (sometimes called “sea” spinach).
Spinach features in many traditional dishes worldwide, from Italian pasta sauces to Indian saag and American salads.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Cooked spinach provides readily absorbable iron that supports normal blood formation.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C act as antioxidants.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked spinach contains about 40 kcal, making it great for weight management.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High vitamin K levels can reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked spinach can be served as a side dish, added to soups, omelets, pasta, or incorporated into casseroles. Before cooking, rinse the leaves and trim thick stems.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh spinach in the refrigerator in an airtight container or bag with a small amount of moisture for 3‑5 days. Cooked spinach keeps in a sealed container in the fridge for 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Swiss steak is a dish that mimics the classic meat‑based Swiss steak but is prepared without any animal protein. Instead of beef, a textured vegetable protein (usually soy or pea) is seared and then braised in a savory gravy made from vegetable broth, tomatoes, and spices. The result is a hearty, saucy entrée suitable for vegetarians and those reducing meat consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “Swiss steak” originally referred to the technique of pounding meat to tenderize it; the meat‑less version uses a gentle “tenderizing” of soy protein.
It is a popular protein‑rich option in school cafeterias across the United States.
The gravy is thickened with flour and cooked in plant‑based oil, making it completely meat‑free.
Traditional recipes marinate the meat in buttermilk; the vegetarian version uses a soy‑sauce and apple‑cider‑vinegar brine.
Meat‑less Swiss steak is often featured in culinary courses focused on sustainable eating.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: Soy or pea protein provides all essential amino acids, supporting muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared with vegetable oil, the dish helps keep cholesterol levels in check.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as soy protein and the vegetable gravy supply B6, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Plant proteins and tomatoes deliver iron and zinc, whose absorption is enhanced by the vitamin C in the sauce.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Tomatoes and other vegetables add dietary fiber that promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals with soy allergy should avoid this dish or use a different plant protein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared gravy can be salty; adjust added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Gluten in the gravy
items.content: If wheat flour is used for thickening, the dish is not suitable for people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the meat‑less Swiss steak hot, ladled with gravy. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, whole‑grain rice, or couscous. Garnish with fresh parsley or dill and a squeeze of lemon for brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps well for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and reheat gently, adding a splash of water or broth if the gravy thickens too much.
